title: Pricing, Release Strategies & Output
intro: How prices are calculated on purchasing documents, how approvals work, and how documents are sent to suppliers.
objectives: Explain the condition technique and the main purchasing condition types
Maintain conditions in info records and condition records
Explain release strategies and flexible workflow
Describe output determination for purchase orders

lessons.title: The condition technique
lessons.body:
Prices on POs are built from conditions using SAP's condition technique, the same logic used in sales pricing.

The building blocks

  • Condition type: one price element, e.g. gross price, discount, freight
  • Condition table: the key a price is stored by (e.g. supplier + material + purchasing org)
  • Access sequence: the order in which tables are searched (most specific first)
  • Condition record: the actual value with validity dates
  • Calculation schema (pricing procedure): sequence of condition types on the document, e.g. standard RM0000

Common condition types

TypeMeaning
PB00 / PBXXGross price (classic); S/4HANA Best Practices systems may use other keys, e.g. PPR0, so check yours
RA01Discount % from gross
RB00Absolute discount
FRA1 / FRB1Freight % / absolute
SKTOCash discount (statistical)

Schema determination

The calculation schema is chosen from the schema group of the supplier (supplier purchasing data) + schema group of the purchasing org. That's why the supplier's schema group field matters.

Use a pizza analogy: base price, discount, delivery charge, total. Everyone gets the condition technique in two minutes.
lessons.narration: Prices on purchase orders are built from conditions, using what SAP calls the condition technique. It's the same logic used in sales pricing. There are five building blocks. A condition type is one price element, like the gross price, a discount, or freight. A condition table defines the key a price is stored by, for example supplier, material and purchasing organisation. An access sequence is the order in which the system searches those tables, most specific first. A condition record is the actual value, with validity dates. And the calculation schema, also called the pricing procedure, is the sequence of condition types that appears on the document. The standard one is R M zero zero zero zero. Common condition types are P B zero zero for gross price in classic configuration, though S/4HANA best practice systems may use other keys, so check yours. R A zero one is a percentage discount, R B zero zero an absolute discount, F R A one and F R B one are freight, and S K T O is cash discount. How is the schema chosen? From the schema group of the supplier, set in the supplier's purchasing data, combined with the schema group of the purchasing organisation. Teaching tip: use a pizza analogy. Base price, discount, delivery charge, total. Everyone understands the condition technique in two minutes.
keyTerms: One price element (gross price, discount, freight)
Pricing procedure for purchasing documents, e.g. RM0000
Supplier/purchasing org key that selects the calculation schema

tryIt.task: Open a PO item in ME23N → Conditions tab. List the condition types, values and the net price.
Click the 'Analysis' button on the conditions tab to see which access found the price.

lessons.title: Maintaining conditions
lessons.body:
Where conditions are stored

  • Info record conditions (most common): price per material–supplier–purchasing org
  • Contract conditions
  • General condition records at other levels: e.g. a supplier-wide discount or a freight charge for a material group

Transactions

  • MEK1 / MEK2 / MEK3: create / change / display conditions
  • ME11 / ME12: info record conditions (Conditions button)
  • MEKE: conditions by supplier (list)

Features

  • Validity periods: future price changes can be entered in advance
  • Scales: quantity- or value-based (e.g. €10 from 1 unit, €9 from 100)
  • Manual conditions added directly on the PO (e.g. one-off freight)

Scales are a great exercise: learners create a scale, then order 50 vs 150 units and watch the price change.
lessons.narration: Conditions can be stored in several places. Most commonly in the info record, as a price per material, supplier and purchasing organisation. They can also be stored in a contract, or as general condition records at other levels, such as a supplier-wide discount or a freight charge for a whole material group. To maintain general conditions, use M E K one, two and three, to create, change and display. Info record conditions are maintained in M E one one or one two, using the conditions button. And M E K E lists conditions by supplier. Three features are worth teaching. Validity periods, so future price changes can be entered in advance. Scales, which are quantity or value based: for example ten euros from one unit, and nine euros from a hundred. And manual conditions added directly on the purchase order, such as a one-off freight charge. Scales make a great exercise: learners create a scale, order fifty units and then a hundred and fifty, and watch the price change.
keyTerms: Price that depends on quantity or value
Date range a condition record applies to
Condition entered directly on the document

tryIt.task: In your info record (ME12), add a scale: €10 from 1 unit, €9 from 100 units.
Create POs for 50 and 150 units and compare the net price.
Add a manual freight condition (FRB1) to a PO item.

lessons.title: Release strategies and approvals
lessons.body:
Companies require approval for purchases above certain values. SAP offers two approaches.

Classic release strategy (classification-based)

  • Characteristics on communication structures: CEBAN for PRs, CEKKO for POs (e.g. total value, purchasing group, plant)
  • Release group and release codes (who approves, e.g. manager, director)
  • Release indicators: blocked, released for PO, changeable after release
  • Release strategy: which codes must approve, in which order, for which values

Release transactions: ME54N / ME55 (PR single / collective), ME29N / ME28 (PO single / collective).

Flexible workflow (S/4HANA)

  • Configured in Fiori: Manage Workflows for Purchase Orders / Purchase Requisitions
  • Conditions (e.g. value above €5,000) and steps (e.g. manager, then purchasing head)
  • Approvers act in the Fiori app My Inbox, also on mobile

A company uses one or the other per document type. Check which before teaching.

For end users, approval training is mostly 'how to approve in My Inbox'. For buyers, it's 'why is my PO blocked and who do I chase?'.
lessons.narration: Most companies require approval for purchases above certain values, and SAP offers two approaches. The classic approach is the release strategy, based on classification. It uses characteristics from communication structures: C E B A N for requisitions and C E K K O for purchase orders, such as total value, purchasing group or plant. Then there are release groups, release codes that represent who approves, release indicators that control what can happen at each stage, and release strategies that define which codes must approve, in which order, for which values. Requisitions are released with M E five four N for one document or M E five five for many. Purchase orders with M E two nine N or M E two eight. The newer S/4HANA approach is flexible workflow. It's configured in Fiori apps, with conditions, such as value above five thousand euros, and steps, such as the manager then the head of purchasing. Approvers act in the Fiori app My Inbox, which also works on mobile. A company uses one approach or the other per document type, so check before you teach. For end users, approval training is mostly how to approve in My Inbox. For buyers, it's why is my purchase order blocked, and who do I chase?
keyTerms: Classic classification-based approval for PRs and POs
Communication structures for PR / PO release characteristics
Approver level in a release strategy
S/4HANA Fiori-configured approval; approvers use My Inbox

tryIt.task: Create a PO above the approval threshold in your system and check the Release strategy tab in ME23N (if it exists).
Release it with ME29N, or approve it in My Inbox if flexible workflow is active.

lessons.title: Output: sending documents to suppliers
lessons.body:
Two output frameworks

  • Classic message determination (NAST): output types such as NEU (new PO) configured with NACE; condition records with MN04; medium print, email, EDI
  • S/4HANA Output Management: based on BRF+ rules, Fiori-friendly forms and email. Default in many new S/4HANA implementations for purchase orders

In practice

  • Output appears on the PO under Messages (ME21N) or the Output Management section (Fiori)
  • Status: not processed, successfully processed, error
  • Re-send or print with ME9F (classic) or from the PO
  • Changes to a PO can trigger change output

Other outputs

RFQs, contracts, scheduling agreement schedules, reminders and return delivery notes all use output too.

Check output status first when a supplier says 'we never received the PO'. It's the most common support call in purchasing.
lessons.narration: Purchase orders reach suppliers through output, and S/4HANA has two output frameworks. The classic one is message determination, where output types such as N E U, for a new purchase order, are configured in N A C E, with condition records maintained in M N zero four. The medium can be print, email or E D I. The newer framework is S/4HANA Output Management, based on B R F plus rules, with Fiori-friendly forms and email. It's the default for purchase orders in many new implementations. In practice, output appears on the purchase order under messages, or in the output management section in Fiori. Each output has a status: not processed, successfully processed, or error. You can re-send or print with M E nine F in the classic framework, or directly from the purchase order. Changes to an order can trigger change output too. And output isn't just for purchase orders: R F Qs, contracts, schedule lines, reminders and return delivery notes all use it. A support tip: when a supplier says they never received the order, check the output status first. It's the most common support call in purchasing.
keyTerms: Classic output type for a new purchase order

tryIt.task: Open your PO and find its output/messages. Check the status.
Preview the PO form (print preview) and identify where header and item data appear.
Trainer kit: script an 'approval workflow demo' from PO creation to approval to output.

flashcards: Supplier schema group + purchasing org schema group

quiz.q: What defines the order in which condition tables are searched?
quiz.explain: The access sequence searches tables from most to least specific.

quiz.q: The calculation schema for a PO is determined by…
options: Supplier and purchasing org schema groups
quiz.explain: Schema determination combines the two schema groups.

quiz.q: Which communication structure holds PO release characteristics?
quiz.explain: CEKKO for POs; CEBAN for PRs.

quiz.q: Approvers using flexible workflow act in…
quiz.explain: Flexible workflow tasks appear in the Fiori My Inbox app.

quiz.q: A price of €10 from 1 unit and €9 from 100 units is a…
quiz.explain: Scales vary price by quantity or value.

quiz.q: Which transaction releases many POs at once (classic)?
quiz.explain: ME28 = collective PO release; ME55 = collective PR release.

quiz.q: A supplier never received a PO. What do you check first?
quiz.explain: Output status shows whether the PO was transmitted.

howToTeach: Pizza analogy for pricing; then open a real PO's conditions tab
Identify early whether the client uses release strategies or flexible workflow
Show an approval on a phone with My Inbox if possible
commonMistakes: Changing price manually on the PO instead of fixing the info record
Not understanding why a PO can't be sent (not yet released)
demoScript: ME12: add a scale; ME21N: show price change by quantity
Create a high-value PO, show block, release/approve
